summary: Expérience AEO : le DR médian des sites cités par les IA est 86 (1 329 sources analysées)
text:
I ran an AEO experiment and found something critical 

the median DR of websites AI cites is 86

I asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude the same set of questions and pulled the DR of all 1,329 sources they cited

say you ask ChatGPT “best CRM for startups”. it searches, reads a bunch of pages, cites around 7 sources and writes you an answer

you read the answer, but the AI read the blog posts first and decided who gets quoted

here’s what the cited pages have in common:

- trust
only 7% of citations came from sites under DR 30

AI quotes sites the web already trusts, and that trust is built with backlinks

- page format
73% of the sources were blog content: listicles, articles and comparisons

product and landing pages were 7%, and forums and social were only 3%

- original data
ChatGPT is the exception: only 18% of its citations were blog content, and 63% were the original source, like a pricing page or the docs

AI quotes the place a fact comes from, so if your post repeats the same stats as 40 other posts, there’s nothing in it to quote

- interactivity on the page
many cited pages had a calculator, chart, table or template

the few humans who click through already read the AI’s summary, so they click to do something, not to read

now you can’t get to DR 86 right away, but you can do 2 things:
1. get to DR 30+ in less than 5 months
2. get your product mentioned in the exact listicles AI keeps citing

Outrank helps you do both 
it builds backlinks for you automatically and gets your product the #1 spot in the listicles AI cites

so after this experiment, we rebuilt all 280 posts on the Outrank blog this week. 275 of them now have a calculator, chart, checklist or template

that’s what we’re building into every Outrank article: real data, backlinks that raise your DR, and pages worth clicking

so now we write for the AI first, then give the human a reason to click

summary: 6 000 tweets analysés : liste courte de ce qui marche sur X aujourd'hui
text:

1. replies beat posts when you're small. your post gets 50 views, a good reply on a viral post can get 50k

2. long beats short, my posts over 600 characters crush my one-liners

3. put a real dollar amount in it, those are my best performers

8. talk about your life more than your product. posts naming my products: 77 likes median. posts about my kids, the chalet, the plane: 167

on top of that, one core rule: be consistent, never miss a day

this is a hard and long journey, you won't win quick, but it's incredibly rewarding if you put in the effort

summary: Origine : les moats se découvrent ; Tweet Hunter est né de son propre usage quotidien, sans audience
text:
moats are discovered, not designed

people tell me I'm successful because of my audience and it's my moat

but when I started building Tweet Hunter, I had no followers

I didn't plan to build a following. I was using my own product every single day, in public, to grow on Twitter

writing threads with it, testing hooks with it, scheduling everything through it

the product needed proof it worked
I was the proof

the audience wasn't a strategy. it was a side effect of one small decision: use the product myself, in public

which is exactly what @robj3d3 is doing with SuperX now

most moats work like that. 
network effects, brand, data, distribution, everything

they look designed when you read about them years later, but they usually start as a small product decision nobody thought was strategic

Cursor didn't start with its own models. it started as an editor people opened every day. the moat came later

Midjourney didn't start with a community moat. it launched inside Discord because it was the fastest way to ship. the moat came later: everyone learned by watching everyone else's prompts

you can't see your moat on day 1 because it doesn't exist yet. it shows up once people actually use the thing

you have to do the work longer than everyone else. then one day you'll see something working for you which is hard to copy

that's the moat

summary: 25 choses que je sais à 45 ans et que j'aurais aimé savoir à 25
text:
25 things I know at 45 that I wish I knew at 25: 

1. Building things that make money is far more rewarding than making money itself.

2. Ideas don’t matter. Execution is everything. Learn how to execute.

3. YOU are going to have to do everything. No one will sign up to execute your “ideas”. (Why would they? You have never actually DONE anything.)

4. Your skills as an entrepreneur will compound over time. Start acquiring them NOW.

5. The quality of your product will dictate how much wind you have at your back.

6. The quality of your team will dictate how far (and fast) you can go. Great talent is everything.

7. You will NEVER regret removing a person from the wrong role. You will only wish you did it sooner.

8. To even have a shot at success, you need a great product AND great marketing. Don’t sleep on either side, or you will never get anything off the ground.

9. Brand is a very real - and very powerful - thing. Learn how to build aspirational brands.

10. Ignore what everybody else is doing. Startups don’t kill startups.

11. Don’t copy people. Figure out how to do SOMETHING new, even in crowded spaces.

12. You don’t actually want wealth. You want freedom, and control over your time and job.

13. Embrace the idea of years (maybe a decade of) “ramen profitability”. Being small will ultimately compound into huge profits (and the freedom you want). It just takes time.

14. The goal is to create the maximum amount of profit with the fewest number of employees.

15. Nobody who is ahead of you can actually give you good advice. They can only share experiences.

16. Set up your life and work so that you can do it for decades without burning out.

17. Learn how to build organic audience on social media ASAP. It will change the trajectory of anything you are doing.

18. Relentless focus on one thing over years and decades is what will make you successful.

19. Let go of the idea of a retirement “number” - because it will always change.

20. A truly great life partner and children will add more to your life than you could ever imagine.

21. Your life will someday be more expensive than you ever thought possible. Don’t fight it - it actually DOES make you happy. Just figure out how to make more money.

22. Consider sobriety. It will really help you, and you will wish you found it sooner.

23. Nutrition is actually far more important than exercise. But exercise > everything else.

24. Never take your foot off the gas. Innovate or DIE.

25. Everything is going to take way longer than you think. Never, EVER give up. 

Just keep building ✌️ | 101 commentaires sur LinkedIn

author: Adam Robinson
summary: Retour : zéro ligne de code sur RB2B depuis 16 semaines et ça grandit encore ; deux raisons
text:
We haven’t touched RB2B code in 16 weeks. We have one CS rep who spends an hour a day on it. Yet it keeps growing. WHY?!?! There are two reasons. One is strategic, the other is philosophical.

Strategic first.

At this point, RB2B has zero real competitors. Plenty of vendors offer person-level website visitor ID (we power most of them). But zero offer only that: nothing else, PLG, 60-second setup, under $100/mo. But nobody else can run this business at this price point.

If you’re VC-backed, a $79/mo high-churn PLG product plateaus. So you have to go upmarket and build more stuff.

If you’re a bootstrapper (like me) and happy with a lean $10M ARR business, you can’t acquire customers for $0 the way I can with my founder brand. And you can’t build and maintain an owned data asset like ours. It costs about $1.5M a year, and we spread that across 3 profitable business units.

So we enjoy our position as the only vendor willing and able to serve an unattractive segment with zero variable cost for our service, priced below everybody else’s CAC.

Now the philosophical part. I think this is the big one.

RB2B has that strategic advantage because of the types of opportunities we choose to pursue as a company. We will not enter a business unless we understand why we have an unfair advantage in one of two ways:

(1) we can either DO something our competitors cannot (thought leadership, expensive data team for cheap product, etc)
(2) we are WILLING to do things our competitors are not (our aggressive position on data privacy - if it’s legal, do it - selling into mid-market and enterprise).

People dismiss RB2B as only possible because of my thought leadership. That might be true. But that’s not the magic of RB2B. 

It’s doing what it’s doing because we looked at the universe of possibility around us when we were designing it and thought “what can only we do, or what are only we WILLING to do”, and made decisions accordingly.

If you’re a founder and you're stuck, ask yourself…

“What can I do that everybody else either can’t, or won’t?” 

Answer that, and you might have a unicorn on your hands..

text:
RB2B is a $10m ARR company with 1 FTE. 

I'd be thrilled if it never grew another dollar.

It's the perfect SaaS for one reason: constraints.

We designed a stupid-simple PLG product that could be supported entirely by Fin. 

The McDonald’s of site visitor ID. 

I know most founders don't agree...

I can’t tell you the number of times - since BEFORE LAUNCH - people told us we needed to use AI to filter for ICP, find more contacts, draft messaging, and send emails and LinkedIn messages. And it’s what all of our competitors did (who are now all DEAD). While we kept the core product in its simplest possible form. 

In fact, it’s STILL HAPPENING. Last week on the way home from our all team offsite in Toronto my buddy Jesse Ouellette was yelling at me about how I needed to roll MoltSets into RB2B because it would solve our churn problem and double revenue. 

But here’s my one question to founders:

WHY DO WE NEED TO SOLVE OUR CHURN PROBLEM AND DOUBLE REVENUE?

If you include our OEM $$$, it’s over $10m ARR. And it requires ALMOST NOTHING from us, while our core team goes on to build something we think has similar characteristics but is even MORE promising. 

Yes, we have a shared data team of 5 people who support four business units that total $32m ARR. Yes, Ebru Abaz does answer escalated tickets, and continues to improve Fin. Yes, Kayley handles OEM. But I am completely baffled that human nature makes it impossible for ANYBODY - even Jesse, a close homie and fellow bootstrapper - to accept that RB2B might just orbit at $10m ARR for the next 5-10 years, its product in its simplest possible form, supported by a SEARINGLY CLEAR value proposition, at a price so low that nobody can disrupt its market position. 

I listened to David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) on David Senra’s podcast on the way to the offsite. Of course I’m a sycophant, he and Jason Fried are my literal heroes. The first book I read when I decided I wanted to be a Founder was Rework. 

In the podcast, DHH made a point about how the HARDEST THING in 2026 as a software founder is to NOT BUILD EVERYTHING, because it’s so easy to build. He said there is something so beautiful about physical products where you finish it, bring it to market, and that’s what it is, on the shelf, forever … And since software isn’t that way, apps often become a bloated mess of noise. 

So I put it to you …

What if RB2B’s revenue doesn’t grow anymore, EVER?

What if the website and product are EXACT same 10 yrs from now? 

What if I launch a brand every 2-3 years that does the exact same thing?

WHY DOESN’T ANYBODY ELSE THINK THAT WOULD BE AWESOME?!?!?!

Because I do. And I’m going to keep doing it.

PS - If you're not using RB2B to identify your anonymous website visitors, you should be. 

Try it free at www.rb2b.com.

summary: Histoire : comment savoir quand pivoter, 3 ans bloqué à 3 M$
text:
Eoin McGuinness: As a founder, how are you able to walk away from an idea that you poured blood, sweat, and tears into for months - or even years? How do you know it's time to pivot?

Me: Because I know what PMF feels like.

Eoin: What do you mean? 

Adam: I spent 3 years stuck at $3m with a product that DIDN’T have PMF. It was miserable. Nothing I tried worked. Then in 2019, we spun out a feature that identified anonymous web traffic. We built it in 8 weeks and in week one I ran $1k of Facebook ads and got $5k MRR back. We were able to get that company to $13m ARR in 2.5yrs w/ 6 people - PRE - AI, and eventually to $23m ARR w/ under 30.

Eoin: Yeah... but how does that make it easy for you to walk away from an idea you’ve chased for months - or even a year - and are SUPER excited about? 

Adam: Because I remember how PAINFUL it was to push on a string. How HARD you can grind and get nothing back. But that experience made me realize that when you have PMF, everything works, it’s NOT a grind … You can still work really hard, but you get back 100x more from every single action than when you don’t have PMF. 

Eoin: What are things that you look for when you are trying to figure out if an idea has the potential for having PMF? 

Adam: I look at facial expressions and mannerisms. If someone is politely nodding their head telling me it sounds smart, it’s a shit idea. If people in the market stop whatever else they are doing, say things like “wait - say that again?” and “when is this out?” and “how can I start using it?” and “how do I buy it?”, I know I’m on the right track. That is what happened with MoltSetsts, which is at $400k ARR, still in beta, no sign up link on site, and we still haven’t invited our entire waitlist.

Eoin: How do you know when to walk away? 

Adam: If 9/10 people that I speak to in the market don’t have some type of “holy shit” reaction to my elevator pitch, at some point I’ll just pull the ripcord on the idea altogether. The length of time depends on my familiarity with the space before I started talking to people. More familiarity is a shorter time, less familiarity, longer time. But the point is - I need UNIVERSAL “HOLY SHIT” reactions to make a product or business out of it. 

Eoin: Have you ever had an idea you regretted walking away from? 

Adam: I regret the 3 years I spent banging my head against the wall as a stuck schmuck at Robly. I WISH I would have had the clarity to realize it wasn’t going to go anywhere no matter what I did. I wish I would have spent time on something that had a chance of actually working. And now, those are the ONLY ideas I spend time on.

text:
5 QUESTIONS THAT ALWAYS MAKE FEEL LIKE SHIT ABOUT MYSELF: 

1. How many employees do you have? (”oh - so you’re just getting started …”)
2. What’s your revenue? 
3. You’re in tech? How much money have you raised? None? Oh.
4. Do you have an office? Oh okay.
5. What’s your company called? Wait - what did you say?

I will say that while this soul-crushing feeling of “smallness” happens less and less to me every year, it still definitely happens. In many worlds (the Aspen YPO chapter, for example), $30m in revenue is peanuts, a team of 30 is tiny, and sadly, in America, size matters, and bigger is better. 

But MAN I remember the PAIN from back in the day, year 2, 3, 4 … 

We only had a couple mm’s in revenue, we were stuck, I had ZERO confidence in myself as a founder, we grew our team to 38, shrunk it to 6, our business was called “Robly” (WHAT?), I had NO IDEA how we were going to get unstuck … and meanwhile I was living in New York in a golden age of VC-backed tech, living in a world of constant anxiety and FOMO, watching EVERYBODY around me absolutely CRUSH IT.

Or so it seemed. 

If you fast forward to today - now 12 years after we launched our first product - if someone actually takes time to understand the details of the operation we have going on, ALMOST NO ONE says anything other than “that’s one of the best businesses I have ever heard of.” 

What changed? 

I just kept building, and along the way there was an external change, and an internal change. 

EXTERNAL: 

The first thing SORT OF worked. $3m ARR, stuck, $10m exit. The second thing worked a bit better. $20m ARR, 25 employees. The third thing REALLY worked. $10m ARR, 3 employees. Now I’m on to the 4th thing, which will probably look a LOT like the 3rd - but we’re still early. 
None of that is mind blowing, but you add it all together, and - at least in my opinion - it actually IS one of the most beautiful businesses in the world. 

INTERNAL: 

I still get the “oh that’s cute” eyes every once in a while, but today I truly believe I have an incredibly beautiful business that gives me energy for other parts of my life, EXACTLY the life I want, and one that I hope to have the privilege of working on for decades to come.

So the eyes don’t sting, because I know I want what I have, even if others who blow me off don’t value it. 

TAKEAWAY

I think it would take a person much more zen than me to rise above the crushing social pressure of being small and stuck at $3m in an environment like NYC in 2015-2020. If you can achieve that level of independent thinking, more power to you. 

For everybody else, my advice is to just keep building. Keep throwing spaghetti at the wall.
If you just keep going, some day you will wake up and realize all of your dreams have come true.

After YEARS of banging my head against the wall, I finally got traction with something COMPLETELY NEW. Well, not completely new. It was an website-ID feature in our original app that I thought was so unique it would get people to use the original app. Which it did not.

If you’re struggling with self doubt, there’s really only one thing you CAN do …

author: Adam Robinson
summary: Les 7 plus grosses erreurs des primo-fondateurs, moi inclus
text:
Most first-time startup founders I talk to set themselves up to fail. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I see nearly EVERY founder make (myself included):

1. You spend too much money on things you don’t really need

People love getting offices, hiring salespeople, getting VA’s, expensive video equipment, software, and even setting up an entity pre-revenue. In 2013, I bought a VOIP phone system a year before we had a customer! Cash will be EXTREMELY tight at some point, even if it’s not now. Remember that.

2. Hiring people before $1m ARR

This is a hot take. I think there should be a technical co-founder building and a business co-founder doing sales, marketing, and support until $1m ARR - just like Klaviyo did. If you have that discipline, you will be profitable, control your destiny, and emerge with product-market fit.

3. Thinking you are an “ideas guy” and can find an operator

I spit out my drink when I hear this. Just like when I hear someone talking about “stealth mode”. Thinking someone will do the hard work for you at this nearly impossible stage is delusional. Once you get to $10m ARR with under 10 people, you earned it, but until then, no way.

4. Not “doing things that don’t scale” under $1m ARR

First-time founders don't understand how manual getting to $1-$3m ARR is. It’s face-to-face conversations, however you can get them, taking the feedback, and improving product as quickly as possible. Nothing will work until the product is great, so all that “growth hacking” will be a waste of time and money.

5. Thinking seed funding means you have a good business

If you were able to raise money for your idea pre-revenue, it means nothing more than you could sell a vision to investors. The hard part is making a business out of it. Keep that in mind and avoid funding at all costs. You’ll thank me later.

6. Not posting on organic social media starting TODAY

This one took me a decade to realize, and a year after I started to master. Nothing is more powerful in today’s world than being able to create great organic social media content that your prospects have demand for independent of what you’re selling. If you start today, you’ll get zero engagement, followers, or leads, but that’s not the point… You’re one day closer to finding your voice.

7. Thinking you’ll be in and out in 3-5 years

Founders should have a decades long time horizon when they start. People wildly overestimate what they can accomplish in a year, but wildly underestimate what they can accomplish over a decade.

TAKEAWAY:

Being a first-time founder is hard.

Literally everything is working against you.

If we knew how hard it was, most would never start.

But here’s the good news...

As Alex Hormozi so elegantly put it:

Every successful person started with:

0 revenue
0 subscribers
0 customers
0 fans

And the only difference between them and everyone else is they actually start.

But that’s not REALLY the secret.

The successful ones not only start…

They keep building.

summary: Histoire : mars 2021, un ingénieur supprime tout le code deux semaines avant un virement de 10 M$, pas de backup
text:
In March of 2021, two weeks before we were supposed to be wired $10m for selling my first bootstrapped startup, one of our engineers accidentally deleted the entire code base - and WE DIDN’T HAVE A BACKUP!!! 

Here’s the full story and how NOT to run your IT at a tiny startup: 

March 26, 2021 was a day like any other. 

I woke up, went for a run, made some coffee, and plugged in for the day.

At around 10am, I got a text from Tate, our CTO.

Tate: “Something really bad just happened.” 

This wasn’t immediately alarming. 

It's a startup. Things always go wrong.

Me: What happened?

Tate: Gustavo (name changed to protect the innocent) deleted the entire code base. 

Me: WHAT?!?!?! How did he do that?

Tate: One of our four nodes crapped out, which has been happening all the time. I taught the guys to go into Amazon and 'reset' it. The problem is there is an option to 'stop' the node directly below the 'reset' option. He chose to 'stop' that one, and just then, by chance, a second node crapped out. He stopped that one two. When you stop two nodes on a 4 node distributed database, it’s all gone.

Me: Well, that sucks, but I guess he didn’t mean to. We have a backup, right?

Tate: No, because to save money, I wasn’t writing a brand new backup file every day because I didn’t want to store two 1TB files. Instead, I would update the old file with the new backup information. There is a two hour window every day where it was writing where if the code base was deleted we wouldn’t have a backup.

I finally began to internalize the meaning of what I was hearing.

My heart started to accelerate and my palms began to perspire.

_____


TIMELINE:

10am: Find this out. 

10:02am: Call co-founder, James, we panic.

10:15am: Call Amazon, they say there is nothing they can do. Ask for someone 
higher up, tell them millions of dollars are on the line.

10:30am: Speak to the higher up person at Amazon, they tell us there is nothing they can do.

10:32am: Tate attempts to reach out to the backup company.

11:00am: Acquirer reaches out and says “your website has been down for a couple hours. Do you know what’s going on?”

11:30am: Tate makes contact with the backup company. They tell him he is an idiot and pennywise and pound foolish for having any time exposed without a complete backup file. Say they can’t help.

11:45am: Tate explains that we are about to sell this for $10m - in literally two weeks - and is able to convince them to connect him with a very senior engineer who actually built the product to see if they can dig into the file somehow. But they had never done this before, so they had no idea. They gave it us a 20% shot they would be able to get the code base back. 

12:00pm: I go to my friend Brad’s house - a VC - who says he has never heard anything like this ever in 30 years of tech, and that Tate had to be plotting something. I said he had 25% of the equity. No way.

***Ran out of space!!

summary: 8 leçons de Russell Brunson, 100 M$ d'ARR bootstrappé en 36 mois
text:
If you’re in SaaS you may not recognize this guy, but every serious entrepreneur needs to study him. Why? Because he bootstrapped his SaaS startup to $100M ARR in just 36 months.

Here are 8 lessons I’ve learned from Russell Brunson and Clickfunnels that you should implement in everything you do, starting today: 

1. Start posting content every day

Russell started a daily podcast in his car on the way to work where he published experiments he was doing, what was working, and what wasn’t. He stuck with it for years and woke up to thousands of fans saying they binged every episode. 

Slowly becoming an “expert” over time created the possibility of $100m ARR.

2. Deeply understand the psychology of your prospects

If you understand the deepest fears and biggest dreams of your prospects, you can create messaging that pierces the hearts of your target audience.

3. Make sure your offer ISN’T incremental

People are not looking for a better version of what’s not working for them. You need to offer a new vehicle.

4. Master one-to-many selling

This was the true unlock, and something no one else has done. Russell was spending $3K driving traffic to a weekly webinar that made on avg $50k in yearly subscriptions. Not kidding.

The secret: he bundled/value stacked info products WITH his SaaS (and positioned the subscription to the SaaS as “free”).

5. Create a category

Russell created a website builder when there were 100s of them, but positioned it as a “sales funnel builder” and had zero competition (for a bit) in that new category.

6. Have ugly branding

The first time I saw the Clickfunnels website, I couldn't believe it. It looked like a kindergartener made it. Like everybody else in SaaS, I blew them off, only to find that it was the fastest growing bootstrapped SaaS ever.

7. Start a movement

Russell studied the biggest movements in history - good and bad - and dialed them down to 3 key components: A charismatic leader, a new opportunity and a future-based cause.

Russell created a tribe called Funnel Hackers and his 2 Comma Club to celebrate the most successful members. He’s a religious-level figure to many.

8. Stay bootstrapped!

Infusionsoft tried to acquire Clickfunnels for $35m early on and VCs were beating the door down. Russell wanted to stay bootstrapped.

TAKEAWAY:

Russell Brunson would crush anything he set out to do

Even so, it’s SHOCKING he could bootstrap $100m ARR selling a $97/mo product to vSMB.

What’s even more insane is that it’s been almost 7 years and no one has tried to replicate his playbook in SaaS.

I believe that Russell’s go-to-market strategy:

1. Driving people to a live event
2. Using an influencer to do one-to-many selling
3. Value-stacking tech with info, tools and templates

…is the future of GTM.

I’m sure sellers of $1M unbudgeted tech will push back and say “no way”.

And maybe for complex and expensive enterprise tech, it's true.

But for everybody else, I have just one question:

Why not?

author: Adam Robinson
summary: Conseils que je donne aux fondateurs : produit disruptif ET marketing disruptif
text:
this is advice I give founders, maybe it helps you:

1/ The only way to experience rapid growth from a cold start is through a disruptive product AND disruptive marketing

2/ Investment capital will NOT help you solve either of the problems of #1 - in most cases it will work against you

3/ Hold off on taking funds from anybody as long as humanly possible. If you absolutely have to raise, do it from people who would give you money if you opened a restaurant

4/ If you can’t raise money from people who would give you money if you opened a restaurant, you aren’t ready yet. Start a simpler business first (consulting, fractional), get some wins

5/ Building a lean, inbound machine that will get you to $10m ARR without many hires, then building a proper company once you are super profitable, you win no matter what

6/ Only hire when it hurts, but let people go the second it seems like someone isn’t the right fit. “I’ve never regretted letting someone go - only not letting them go soon enough”

7/ Start working with an executive coach at $5m ARR to help you learn how to communicate and manage people. You suck at it, have horrible habits, and it will take years to change them

8/ If you are stuck at 1%’s growth at $1m ARR, raising money will not fix that problem. You will likely need to pivot to something totally new and different to grow

9/ If you can hold out on investment long enough, the freedom you will have as a bootstrapper will give you the life you wanted when you started on this path in the first place. VC will not

Just my two cents. 

Hope it helps.

summary: Jour 2 : retour d'une PM sur le modèle patient, cas limites intégrés
text:
Day 2: Building Prima - a system that handles real clinical situations, not just forms for PHCs

Yesterday I posted my Patient model. I thought it was complete.

Then, Blessing Nwoji, a Product Manager in EdTech and HealthTech, left this feedback:

"I think edge cases for gender should be included eg female - (para & gravida). If this includes children, immunization record should be included."

That one comment made me re-think the whole database.

In a real PHC in Enugu / Anambra, 60% of the register is ANC and immunization. If my system can't handle that, it's useless.

So here's what I built today:

1. For Female Patients - ANC Ready:
Added para, gravida, isPregnant to Patient.
 •  Gravida = number of pregnancies
 •  Para = number of births
 •  This is critical for antenatal care.

2. For Children Under 5 - Immunization Ready:
Created a new ImmunizationRecord table linked to Patient. Each record stores vaccine name (BCG, Penta etc.), dose number, date given, and next due date. So a nurse can see who is due next.

3. What I'm most proud of - Making it PHC-proof:

 •  Human-readable IDs like ANK-00042, not random strings. Nurses need to write it on a card.
 •  Counter is atomic. If 2 nurses register at the same time, they never get duplicate numbers.
 •  Age is not stored. I store DOB and calculate age. For babies, it shows "8 months" not "0 years".
 •  Search from ONE box: name, phone, NHIS, or card number. Even if you type phone with spaces.
 •  Duplicate protection: If Chukwudi, 2019-05-01, Nando village already exists, it warns you instead of creating double entry.

And most important: All clinical rules live on the SERVER, not just the form.

 •  Male marked as pregnant? Rejected (400).
 •  10-year-old with gravida? Rejected.
 •  Para > Gravida? Rejected - you can't have more births than pregnancies.
 •  Vaccine date before birth date? Rejected.
 •  Immunization record for a 20-year-old? Rejected.

Hiding a field in UI is not security. Real validation is server-side.

Tested with 10+ REST Client requests - success, conflicts, bad phone numbers, future DOB like Feb 31.

Thank you so much Blessing Nwoji for that feedback! You made this system actually usable for a PHC. You spotted what I would have missed.



Health workers, PMs - What else does a PHC nurse need at registration that I'm still missing?

Day 1: Building a Patient Registration System for PHCs

What I did today:

I set up Next.js with TypeScript, Tailwind, Prisma and PostgreSQL.

The real work was thinking through the patient fields.

At first I just wanted name, age, phone. But then I remembered my PHC visits:

If a mother comes from a village with no phone, how do we reach her? That's why I added Next of Kin + Village/LGA.

If a patient has NHIS, we need NHIS number.

If a patient has allergies, the nurse must see it instantly before prescribing.

So my Patient table now has: Full Name, DOB (age auto-calculates), Gender, Phone, Address/Village, LGA, State, Next of Kin, NHIS No (optional), Blood Group, Known Allergies, Registration Date, PHC Name.

It looks simple, but designing it right is 50% of the work. A bad schema = lost records tomorrow.

What I learned today:

In health data, every field must answer "why does a nurse in a rural PHC need this at 9pm with no light?"

summary: Curation : citation de Karpathy, le client n'est plus l'humain mais l'agent
text:
Andrej Karpathy dropped this recently:

"The customer is not the human anymore. It's agents acting on behalf of humans."

And honestly, I see it happening in my own business already.

My own AI agents already interact with Stripe, Notion, GitHub, n8n, and a dozen other tools on my behalf. They read APIs, process webhooks, make decisions, and take action. I never open half of these dashboards anymore.

Now multiply that by every founder, every team, every company adopting AI agents in the next 2-3 years.

Suddenly your beautiful UI does not matter as much. Your onboarding wizard is irrelevant. Your 14 dashboard tabs are wasted effort.

What matters is:

1. How good is your API?
Agents do not click buttons. They call endpoints. If your API is an afterthought (or does not exist), you are invisible to the fastest-growing segment of "users."

2. How clean is your data model?
Agents need structured, predictable data. The messier your backend, the harder it is for an agent to work with your product reliably.

3. How fast can an agent get value?
Forget time-to-value for humans. What is the time-to-value for an agent? Can it authenticate, fetch data, and take action in under 30 seconds? Or does it need to navigate a cookie banner first?

I am not saying UI is dead. Humans still need interfaces for complex decisions, creative work, and oversight.

But I am saying that in 2-3 years, a huge chunk of your "active users" will be agents. And most products are completely unprepared for that.

The SaaS companies that win the next wave will be the ones who treat agents as first-class users. Not an API docs page buried in the footer.

I am already rebuilding parts of my own products with this in mind. If Karpathy is right (and I think he is), this shift will be just as big as the mobile shift was 15 years ago.

Except this time, the new "user" does not care about your brand colors.

author: Alex Lieberman
summary: 25 bootcamps d'agents IA en 90 jours : liste des leçons
text:
We've run AI agent bootcamps with 25+ enterprises over the last 90 days. 

The point of a bootcamp is to go from AI use case to deployed agent in 2 weeks. 

We've learned a shit ton from these deployments so far. 

Here's the laundry list of lessons: 

1) Many enterprises require on-prem or self-hosted deployment for agents in production.

2) Executives being bought in & motivated to get agents into production is critical. Without VP+ sponsorship, things won't move fast or cross the finish line. 

3) Data access is the #1 challenge. IT and security teams are paid to protect data and access which is right, a lot of this data is sensitive. However, those incentives block AI adoption more than anything else. 

4) People don't know what they want. Once you understand a workflow, you keep finding new ways to extend the agent into functions that the stakeholder had not considered.

5) Processes that aren't standardized aren't automateable. It's best to roll out processes, then automate them.

7) The goal should be to automate a function, not a single person.

8) Once you have automated one function, bottlenecks still exist in others and if you can build agents that work across functions, they are able to compound in new ways.

9) ROI is very hard to estimate, but there are often business cases with clear value. Saved time as an ROI metric is great, however, there is potentially more value in where that person's time is reallocated.

10) People still want an interface. We thought that the agent doing the work and acting like a coworker was enough, but we are hearing they need to see a dashboard and visualizations of the data and what the agent is doing.

11) Front load as many conversations with users as possible. Its often that leaders might have only high level understanding of a workflow. The users are always the people you want to ask questions to.

12) Talking to one person isn't enough per use case. Each person has their own way of doing things. While we may build something good, if its not clearly better or handles nuance for people, adoption will fail. 

13) Start building ASAP. The quicker you show the stakeholder something, the quicker you can get feedback and pivot. 

14) Be the "dumb" person in the room. Ask the dumb questions, deeply understand the workflow/use case, because you can't truly build or articulate the value of something if you don't understand the problem and solution.

15) Different stakeholder care about different things. Workflow owners want to understand the nitty gritty detail of the agent and workflow. Executives care less about the demo and more about the savings, the transformation, the vision.

16) AI is getting really good, where in the past, you might have needed a ton of extra functionality/code around the agent. As the models get better, the agent can do more and more of the work.

summary: A construit un explicatif interactif : où vont vos 20 $ d'abonnement Claude
text:
You pay $20 a month for Claude. Where does that money actually go?

I built an interactive explainer (link below) that follows one prompt, “How does AI work?”, from your keyboard down to the bedrock. 

Here’s the walkthrough:

1) Type the prompt ($0). 
- Your question gets chopped into about 5 tokens.           
- Claude also reads thousands of tokens of its own standing instructions (aka system prompt)

2) Pay Claude ($13.00). 
- Anthropic keeps about 65% of your $20. 
- That funds training the next model, research and the people. 

3) Down the fiber ($0.02). 
- Your tokens travel as light through glass cables. 
- Round trip: about 40 milliseconds.

4) Rent a GPU ($2.48).
- The cloud is a landlord for computers. 

5) Keep it cool ($0.84). 
- A modern AI rack of 72 GPUs draws 120 to 140 kW, about what 100 US homes use.
- Nearly all of it turns into heat.

6) Claude thinks ($0). 
- It writes the answer one token at a time, about 700 of them in ~12 seconds.

7) Chips do the math ($2.88). 
- Every token takes billions of multiplications. 
- Chip, memory and network makers get paid here.

8) Print the chip ($0.30). 
- That chip was printed months earlier, layer by layer with ultraviolet light, almost certainly by TSMC.

9) Send the power ($0.41). 
- Tiny slice, biggest bottleneck. 
- New grid hookups can take 5 to 7 years.

10) Hold it all up ($0.07). 
- Land, steel, copper and concrete get the last few cents.

Play around with the explainer for free: https://lnkd.in/eDQF862x

summary: 11 principes de construction d'audience appris chez Morning Brew
text:
11 audience-building principles I learned building Morning Brew into a $75m co with tens of millions of followers....

Hope they help: 

1) Content is a compounding asset when done right. You expend 80% of your effort to create something great once and then expend the remaining 20% to distribute it hundreds of times. 

2) The best type of distribution businesses are IP businesses. Disney is an IP business. WWE is an IP business. An IP business treats creative concepts or characters as core financial assets rather than standalone entertainment products. 

3) To build distribution is to be an asset manager of attention, finding dislocations in the market & allocating attention across a portfolio of rented (social), owned (email/pod/community), and monetized audience. 

4) AI should be used relentlessly to earn distribution & yet the end user should never feel it. If they do feel it, either you've used AI lazily or lack taste. 

5) Curation has never been more important. Thx to the internet, social platforms, and AI the cost of creating content is basically zero. That means content supply has gone exponential. But attention is decidedly finite. 

6) The internet rewards novelty. Either say original things in old ways or old things in original ways. 

7) Media companies are great at generating attention, but suck at harvesting it. Non-media companies suck at generating attention, but are great at harvesting it. 

8) Riches are in the niches. We went from 12 channels on the original TVs to near unlimited choice. And in a world of unlimited choice, consumers can find great content related to any/all interests from the most mainstream to the most obscure.

9) We are late stage on most content platforms. In the early days of Instagram, Tiktok, and Twitter, attention was cheap, and you could amass a large audience simply by being an early adopter and actively creating on-platform. Those days are (mostly) gone. This means that the quality bar for what is “worthy” of a consumer’s time continues to increase.

10) You are only as successful as your last post. Social platforms were built on the social graph. You see the content of the people you follow and your content is seen by people that follow you. Interest graphs (made popular by TikTok) flipped digital media on its head. The variance of performance has never been higher, and it’s never been easier for someone with a small audience to get outsized results on a single piece of content.

11) Software is becoming content. As the barriers to build software approach 0, software is a new content medium which can be used to build and own audience.

- Apps are losing ground. App funding grew only about 18% in 2026, from roughly $61B to $72B, while total AI funding more than doubled. That cut apps' share of AI money roughly in half, from about 29% to about 15%. Vertical apps like Harvey actually shrank, from about $17B to $11B.

author: Alex Lieberman
summary: Hot take : les evals sont ce qui bloque les entreprises, guide en newsletter
text:
Hot take: evals are the #1 thing keeping companies from becoming AI-native. 

If you want to understand evals, read this post & then the accompanying guide. 

Tweaking prompts and trying a few inputs by hand only gets you so far; evals are what get your agents ready for deployment and keep them working once they're live.

First, some definitions...

- An eval: a grader applied to a trace.
- A grader: anything that scores how well the agent did, from a simple code check to an LLM acting as a judge. 
- A trace: the full record of one agent run: the input, every step it took, and the output. For example, a customer asks "Where is my refund?" The agent calls search_orders, then issue_refund, and replies "Refund sent, 3–5 days."

Next, let's dive into graders... 

Graders come in a few families, and most real setups run several on the same trace.
1) Deterministic checks. Plain code, no model involved. Did the agent call issue_refund exactly once, with the same order ID it looked up? A double refund or a refund on the wrong order fails instantly.
2) Reference-answer graders. Compare the output to a reference answer stored on the case, by exact match or with an LLM judge checking whether the meaning matches.
3) Rubric graders. An LLM judge scores the output against criteria, with no reference answer needed. Is the reply concise? Does it confirm what happened?
4) Trajectory graders. These grade the steps the agent took, not just its final answer. Did it look up the order before issuing the refund? A run that calls issue_refund without checking the order first fails even if the final reply reads perfectly.

What are online vs. offline evals? 

Online evals watch production. Offline evals run in your lab: on demand or in CI, before anything ships.
- You need both. Online without offline means you can see problems but can't fix them safely. - Offline without online means you're testing the scenarios you imagined, not the ones your users actually create.
- What connects the two is promotion, turning a bad production trace into an offline case.

Next, eval-driven development...

Eval-driven development is test-driven development for agent behavior.
1) Define the case and its pass criteria.
2) Run it and watch it fail.
3) Change the agent.
4) Run it again. Repeat steps 3 and 4 until it passes.
5) Run the full dataset, not just this case, to catch regressions.

Run each case several times (k) and set the bar explicitly: all-of-k for high-stakes behavior where a single failure is unacceptable, or n-of-k, like 2 of 3, where some variance is acceptable.

Put together, online evals find a problem, promotion turns it into a case, the loop fixes it offline, and the growing dataset makes sure it stays fixed.

text:
I chatted with Connor - a 23 year old who vibe-coded an app in under 2 weeks and grew it to $20K/month in 50 days.

His apps have done over $1M in revenue. 

Without a CS degree. 
And completely solo. 

He learned to code by watching YouTube and grinding on Stack Overflow.

His latest app is called Payout. It’s a simple list of class action lawsuits you might be owed money from. You tap one, fill out a form, the app preps the PDF, you mail it in.

That’s the whole product.

He entered RevenueCat’s hackathon (55,000+ entrants), grew Payout to $20K/month over the 2-month window, and won the $65K Build & Grow grand prize.

His playbook in 4 steps:

1. Steal design taste. Download 20 apps in the niche, screenshot every onboarding screen, line them up in Figma, remix the best parts.

2. Obsess over onboarding. 90% of users never see past it. Invoke emotion, make it feel personal, add charts so it feels scientific.

3. Vibe code the core first. Write a text doc + JSON of your data structures, drop screenshots into Claude Code, skip the onboarding, ship the main feature fast.

4. Pick ideas that tap core human desires - health, money, looks. Payout works because “people will spend money on an app that makes them more money.”

Growth was just as lean: one UGC creator in-niche → thousands of downloads → turn the winning organic videos into Facebook ads.

The takeaway: “A simple app can make lots of money. You only really need 1 to 3 good features, and your onboarding will pull most of the way for you.” | 22 commentaires sur LinkedIn

summary: Histoire d'un tiers : 25 k$/mois en 15 mois sans marketing
text:
I sat down with Avneesh a solo founder who built a $25,000/month business in just 15 months without spending a dime on marketing.

His product is SaveWise: 

a tool that helps people stack credit card points and airline miles on stuff they’re already buying online.

When he launched, he did what every founder does. 

Product Hunt. 
Hacker News. 
Indie Hackers. 

Tons of traffic... and a 95–96% bounce rate. Then he emailed 300–400 influencers. 

He got ONE reply.

So he flipped the strategy. Instead of chasing builders, he went where his actual customers hung out on Reddit and Facebook groups about travel and credit card points.

His 5-step playbook:
1. Brainstorm 10–15 keywords/interests your customer cares about (he used “Map of Reddit” to find adjacent subreddits)

2. Lurk first - never post immediately. Learn the etiquette

3. Set a clear goal for each community before posting

4. Set keyword alerts with F5bot so you catch every relevant convo in real time

5. Be ridiculously helpful in the comments - earn the right to mention your product

The proof? He found a Facebook group called “Rakuten Stacks.” Wrote a SQL query, dumped the data into a Google Sheet, dropped the link. 1,500+ people clicked through to his site from a single post.

On Reddit, he lurked a community for weeks, posted in weekly Q&A threads for 3.5 months, built what people asked for, then DM’d the mod for permission to do a top-level post. It blew up.

Today: tens of thousands of users, 1,500 paying customers, and 97% of revenue comes from a lifetime plan customers literally begged him to create.

Takeaway: knowing your customer isn’t just for what to build - it’s for knowing exactly where to find them.

12 months later, Kelechi has built two apps that did $1.5M in revenue.

His first app, Social Wizard, is an AI dating assistant that helps guys reply to Instagram stories. The idea came from a girl on his failed photo-sharing app Caspade he couldn't figure out what to text her, so he wrote a NestJS script using OpenAI to generate flirty lines.

He showed it to his high school friends at Homecoming. For the first time ever, they actually cared about something he built. That was the signal.

First sale: $10 in late January.

Two weeks after cracking distribution: $3.5K MRR.

One month later: $25K MRR.

Six months in: $250K cash collected.

Year one: ~$500K cash collected.

The crazy part? $0 spent on traditional marketing.

His secret was what he calls the "streamer strategy." He paid micro-streamers (Fortnite kids, reaction creators not even in his niche) $120 per video to demo the app on a real girl's Instagram story. One video hit 2M views and brought in tens of thousands of dollars.

Then he built Clean Eats, a barcode scanner that tells women how a food affects their skin. Hit $10K in 2 weeks. Sold it to a UK company 4 months later.

His take: "Distribution is a show-don't-tell game. If you put out 100 videos a day, that's 700 a week. If one goes viral, that's not luck."
